Low-Rank Adaptation and its quantized successor QLoRA open this short series on training and fine-tuning advances between 2023 and 2025. The intuition behind LoRA is that although a pretrained weight matrix W0 is large, the update needed to specialize a model for a new task tends to have low intrinsic rank, so most adaptation signal lives in a small subspace. Rather than learning that update directly, LoRA factorizes it as the product of two smaller matrices, B of shape d×r and A of shape r×k with r far smaller than min(d,k), and freezes W0 entirely. The forward pass through an adapted layer becomes h = W0x + BAx, so training touches only A and B while the base model's weights never need gradients computed or stored. B is initialized to zero and A to a random Gaussian, guaranteeing the update BA is exactly zero at the start of training. Because W0 + BA can be recombined into a single matrix before deployment, and swapped for a different B′A′ pair for another task, LoRA lets one base model serve many specialized adapters at minimal storage overhead. QLoRA extends this by compressing the frozen base model to 4-bit precision using NormalFloat4, a data type whose quantization bins concentrate near the centre of the weight distribution to match the roughly Gaussian shape of pretrained weights. To limit the resulting error, QLoRA computes a separate quantization constant per block of weights rather than one per tensor, then quantizes those constants themselves in a second pass called double quantization, trimming memory further. It also uses gradient checkpointing and paged optimizers to keep activation-gradient memory from spiking while gradients flow through the frozen quantized weights into the full-precision adapters, the only parameters actually updated. The practical payoff is that models once requiring multi-GPU clusters to adapt can be fine-tuned on far more modest hardware, with task-switching costing megabytes of adapter weights rather than a full checkpoint. The open question sits mostly in the knobs: choosing rank r trades approximation fidelity against overfitting when data is scarce, and how aggressively to quantize remains an active design choice. Direct Preference Optimization is the second technique here, and it let alignment teams skip the reinforcement-learning stage of RLHF entirely. Standard RLHF fits a reward model to preference comparisons via the Bradley-Terry model and a classification loss, then runs an RL stage maximizing that reward while a KL term keeps the policy near a reference model, a three-phase pipeline that is complex and often unstable. DPO's central move is that the KL-constrained reward-maximization problem has a closed-form solution: the KL divergence between a candidate policy πθ(y|x) and the distribution (1/Z(x))πref(y|x)exp((1/β)r(x,y)) is, by Gibbs' inequality, minimized at zero exactly when the two distributions coincide, so the optimal policy π* equals that normalized, reward-tilted reference distribution. Because that expression is intractable to use directly, since Z(x) requires summing over every possible string, it is rearranged to write the reward as r(x,y) = β log πr(y|x)/πref(y|x) + β log Z(x), turning a statement about rewards into one about a policy and a reference policy. Substituting this reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry probability p(y1≻y2|x) = σ(r(x,y1) − r*(x,y2)) makes Z(x) cancel out of the difference, leaving preference probability expressed purely through the optimal and reference policies, with no reward model involved. That yields a maximum-likelihood objective directly over the policy's parameters, trained by ordinary supervised learning with a negative log-likelihood loss over an offline dataset of prompts paired with preferred and dispreferred completions sampled from the reference policy. The benefit is threefold: no reward model needs training, no reinforcement-learning loop is required, and the policy is optimized on preferences using a well-understood supervised procedure instead of a fragile one. Its documented weaknesses include dependence on paired preference data that is not always easy to collect, sensitivity to label noise since it cannot account for a flipped preference, and an inability to sample fresh preference pairs from the current optimal policy because it never fits an explicit reward model. These gaps motivated KTO, which drops paired data by maximizing a Kahneman-Tversky value function over individually labeled examples, RSO, which uses statistical rejection sampling to better approximate preference data from the target optimal policy, and IPO and conservative DPO, which resist over-optimizing away from the reference model during long training. Mixture-of-Experts architecture is the third advance covered here, and it decouples a model's total parameter count from the compute spent per token. The intuition is conditional computation: instead of pushing every token through one dense feed-forward block, an MoE layer keeps n parallel expert networks and a gating network outputting a vector G(x) scoring each expert's relevance to the current token. The layer's output is a weighted sum of the experts' outputs weighted by G(x), and a top-K gating rule restricts this sum to the K highest-scoring experts by applying a softmax to only the top-K logits of a linear layer, so K can be far smaller than n while the model still holds the full parameter space. Mixtral 8x7B applies this by giving each transformer layer eight expert blocks in place of one, routing every token to its top two experts, so the model carries 47 billion total parameters but activates only about 13 billion to process any given token. Because each expert can be assigned to a different accelerator through expert parallelism, sparse MoE layers fit naturally onto multi-GPU training and serving. The open challenge on the training side is load balancing: ensuring an even distribution of tokens across experts is necessary to prevent bottlenecks and make full use of available compute, and it remains flagged as a genuine engineering concern rather than a solved problem.

Low-Rank Adaptation and its quantized successor QLoRA open this short series on the training and fine-tuning advances that reshaped large language models between 2023 and 2025.

The motivating intuition behind LoRA is that although a pretrained weight matrix W0 is large, the update needed to specialize a model for a new task tends to have low intrinsic rank, so most of the adaptation signal lives in a small subspace.
Rather than learning that update directly, LoRA factorizes it as the product of two much smaller matrices, B of shape d×r and A of shape r×k with r far smaller than min(d,k), and freezes W0 entirely. [00275]
The forward pass through an adapted layer becomes h = W0x + BAx, so training touches only A and B while the base model's weights never need gradients computed or stored. [00275]
B is initialized to zero and A to a random Gaussian, which guarantees the update BA is exactly zero at the start of training. [00275]
Because W0 + BA can be recombined into a single matrix before deployment, and swapped for a different B′A′ pair for another task, LoRA adds no inference latency and lets one base model serve many adapters. [00275]
QLoRA extends this by first compressing the frozen base model to 4-bit precision using NormalFloat4, a data type whose quantization levels match the roughly Gaussian distribution of pretrained weights. [03514]
To limit the resulting error, QLoRA computes a separate quantization constant for every block of weights rather than one constant per tensor, then quantizes those constants themselves in a second pass, called double quantization, trimming memory further without materially hurting accuracy. [03514]
During training, the 4-bit weights are dequantized on the fly so gradients can flow through the frozen quantized base model into the still full-precision LoRA adapters, which are the only parameters updated. [03514]
The practical payoff is that models once requiring multi-GPU clusters can be fine-tuned on a single workstation GPU, with task-switching costing megabytes rather than a full checkpoint. [00275] [03514]
The open questions are about the knobs rather than the mechanism: rank r trades fidelity against overfitting when data is scarce, and quantization precision continues to be probed by later variants such as QA-LoRA. [03514]

Direct Preference Optimization is the second technique in this series, and it let teams skip the reinforcement-learning stage of RLHF entirely.
Standard RLHF fits a reward model to preference comparisons via a Bradley-Terry classification loss, then runs PPO to maximize that reward while a KL penalty keeps the policy near a reference model, a three-stage pipeline that is expensive and unstable to tune. [02738]
DPO's central move is that the KL-constrained reward-maximization problem solved in the RL stage has a closed-form solution: minimizing the KL divergence between a candidate policy and the distribution (1/Z(x))πref(y|x)exp((1/β)r(x,y)) is, by Gibbs' inequality, zero exactly when the two distributions coincide, so the optimal policy equals that normalized, reward-tilted reference distribution. [00100]
Rearranging this closed form expresses the reward itself as r(x,y) = β log(πr(y|x)/πref(y|x)) + β log Z(x), turning any reward function into an equivalent statement about a policy and a reference policy. [02738]
Substituting this reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry probability p*(y1≻y2|x) = σ(r*(x,y1) − r*(x,y2)) makes the intractable partition function Z(x) cancel, leaving preference probability expressed purely through the optimal and reference policies. [02738]
That yields a maximum-likelihood objective directly over the policy's own parameters, training it to increase log πθ(yw|x)/πref(yw|x) relative to the same ratio for a losing response yl, through a binary cross-entropy loss whose sigmoid is inherited from the Bradley-Terry model. [02738] [00818]
Because this is ordinary supervised classification over a fixed offline preference dataset, DPO needs no reward model, no on-policy sampling, and no RL infrastructure, while implicitly optimizing the same objective RLHF pursues. [02738]
It has been used to align open instruction-tuned models, including Mixtral's instruct variant, and is generally reported as more stable and data-efficient than PPO-based RLHF. [02738]
Its known weaknesses include overfitting to near-deterministic preference pairs at the expense of the KL term, and a mismatch between the reward optimized during training and the metric used at generation, gaps that later methods such as KTO, RSO, cDPO, and IPO were each built to address differently. [00818]

Mixture-of-Experts architecture is the third advance covered here, and it decouples a model's total parameter count from the compute spent per token.
The intuition is conditional computation: instead of pushing every token through one dense feed-forward block, an MoE layer keeps several parallel expert feed-forward networks and a learned router that sends each token to only a handful of them, so the model holds far more total parameters while per-token compute stays small. [01343]
Mixtral 8x7B, released by Mistral AI in December 2023, replaces the feed-forward sub-block of each transformer layer with eight expert networks of 7B parameters each, and for every token a gating network selects the top two experts and combines their outputs as a weighted sum, with the gate's own output supplying the weights. [01343]
Everything outside these MoE layers, including attention, is shared and computed densely, so the active computation per token corresponds to only a fraction of the model's total parameters, and because each layer's experts can sit on separate devices, the architecture fits naturally onto model-parallel training and serving. [01343]
The practical benefit is a model that reaches or beats the quality of a much larger dense network while running inference at roughly the speed and cost implied by its active rather than total parameter count. [01343]
The open challenges sit in training and serving rather than the forward pass itself: every expert must still reside in accelerator memory even though only a couple are used per token, so VRAM requirements resemble the dense model's total size, and Mixtral's own authors note that training and data management for such models remain harder than for a comparably capable dense network. Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

Posted by JacksonCakes on October 1, 2023

Given the rapid advancements in large language models (LLMs) like the recent launch of Llama 2 and research focusing on parameter efficiency, hallucination reduction, and accelerated inference, we're seeing the gap close between open-source models and commercial solutions like ChatGPT. Companies today often don't require a Jack-of-all-trades language model capable of solving complex mathematical equations; they're looking an LLM that excel at specific tasks relevant to their domain. Fine-tuning a large language model on a custom dataset is increasingly becoming a practical and efficient choice. That's why I'm launching a series called 'Road to Efficient LLMs,' where I'll explore the latest techniques for fine-tuning and optimizing these powerful models for real-world applications. Note: While you can certainly fine-tune models like GPT-3.5, having your own large language model offers greater flexibility and can be more cost-effective for experimentation.

Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) are undoubtedly powerful, thanks to their extensive training on massive amount of datasets. However, their generalized knowledge isn't always sufficient for specialized tasks that demand high accuracy. The good news is, you don't have to start from scratch to make them domain-specific experts. A few epochs of focused training, known as fine-tuning, can do the trick. Yet, the enormous size of these models (Currently,largest open-source model to is Falcon with 180 billions parameters), makes fine-tuning a daunting task on consumer-grade GPUs. Today, we'll explore one of the solution to this challenge: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models.
Note: While our focus is on LLMs, it's worth noting that this method can be applied to any neural network with weight matrices.

Background concepts

Before delving into the explanation of LoRA, it's crucial to grasp the concepts of matrix rank and decomposition. Simply put, the rank of a matrix is the number of linearly independent rows or columns, or in other words, number of unique rows (that are not made from other rows, same concept applied to column as well). To demystify this definition, consider a straightforward example.

Upon examination, it's evident that the second row is thrice the first, which implies that Matrix $X$ has only one unique row, rendering it a rank 1 matrix. In order word, it only have one unique row or rank 1. Consequently, $X$ can be decomposed into two smaller matrices, $A$ and $B$, with dimensions $2×1$ and $1×3$, respectively:

Now, instead of having a full-rank matrix $X$, we could represent it with two low-rank matrices matrix $A$ and $B$ which closely resemble the original full-rank matrix $X$. As another example, consider a matrix of size 1000 * 1000, We could approximate it with two matrices of sizes $1000 * 100$ and $100 * 1000$, where 100 is the rank. This approach reduces the number of elements in the matrix from 1,000,000 -> 100,000+100,000. More formally, for a matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, we could decompose it into two matrix $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k}$, where $r \ll \min (d, k)$.
Note: The example above can be applied to columns as well.

LoRA

Concepts

LoRA is build on top of the hypothesis that state:

..the change in weights during model adaptation also has a low "intrinsic rank"

This implies that updates to the original weight matrices can be represented as low-rank matrices. Recap the previous section, suppose $W \in \mathbb{R}^{1000 \times 1000}$ represents the updates to the original weight matrix. This matrix could be approximated by two other matrices with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{1000 \times 10}$ and $A \in \mathbb{R}^{10 \times 1000}$. Training matrices $A$ and $B$ can therefore approximate the weights derived from full fine-tuning. The forward pass of a model (assuming it is a single layer) can be formally expressed with the following equation:

\[h=W_0 x+\Delta W x=W_0 x+B A x\]

where $h$ is the output of current layer, $W_0$ is the original pre-trained weights (frozen), $\Delta W$ is the update of original weights, $BA$ is the low-rank weight and $x$ is the input.

To better understand, refer to the visuals provided above. Given input $X \in \mathbb{R}^{d}$, the left segment (depicted in blue) represents the original pre-trained weights $W \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$,while the right segment (in orange) showcases two low-rank matrices $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$. During inference, we could add the original weights and matrix $BA$ to get output $h$ as describe in previous equation.
Note: They use a random Gaussian initialization for A and zero for B, so ∆W = BA is zero at the beginning of training.

Advantage of LoRA

Memory and Storage Efficiency: Since updates aren't performed on the original weight matrices, only the gradients of the low-rank weight matrices need to be stored. As such, the gradients of the pre-trained, frozen weights are neither required nor calculated. This approach is particularly efficient when dealing with low-rank matrices, resulting in significant reductions in memory and storage requirements. For a more technical explanation, please refer the discussion here.

Able to switch between task. Consider a scenario involving a model with 170 billion parameters intended for use on multiple downstream tasks. Storing multiple models of this size is not only costly but also inefficient. However, with fine-tuned adapters designated for each task, switching between tasks can be accomplished with minimal memory overhead. We could simply substract $W$ with $BA$ to recover the original weights and adding a different $B^{\prime} A^{\prime}$.

Implementation

Pretrained Model

As LoRA is primarily utilized for fine-tuning large models, we will begin by implementing a simplified model that will act as our "pre-trained model". For the sake of simplicity, this model will be trained using the CIFAR-10 dataset.

At the core of QLoRA is the concept of low-rank adaptation (LoRA), which involves inserting small, low-rank matrices (adapters) between the layers of a pre-trained model.
These adapters capture the essential transformations needed for a specific task while keeping the model complexity low.
By decomposing the weight matrices into lower-rank representations, LoRA enables efficient fine-tuning of LMs by focusing on updating the adapters instead of the entire model.
Quantization Techniques and Memory Efficiency
QLoRA takes the concept of low-rank adaptation further by introducing quantization techniques to reduce memory usage and computational requirements.

Unlike traditional quantization methods that use a single constant for all weights, QLoRA computes separate quantization constants for each block of weights, ensuring a more accurate and nuanced quantization.
The quantization constants play a crucial role in this process, serving as scaling factors to map the quantized values back to their original range during dequantization.

Definitions

Dense Feed-forward Layers: These layers are standard components in neural networks where each input is connected to each output by a learned weight. In the context of transformer architectures, dense feed-forward layers are present within each transformer block and process the input sequentially, applying the same set of weights across the entire sequence.

Router: In the context of a Mixture of Experts (MoE) layer, a router is a mechanism that determines how the input is distributed among the various experts. It takes each token or piece of input data, computes a probability distribution over the experts, and routes the input to the selected experts based on this distribution. The routing process is crucial for managing the computational load and ensuring that the most relevant experts handle each piece of input.

Decoder-only Architecture: This architecture refers to transformer models that only use the decoder component, omitting the encoder. In autoregressive large language models (LLMs), the decoder-only architecture is prevalent, where each transformer block within the decoder contains layers for masked self-attention and feed-forward processing. The architecture is designed to generate output one token at a time, using previously generated tokens as context.

Sparse Activation: This concept refers to the activation of only a small subset of the available experts in an MoE layer for any given input. Despite the MoE layer having a large number of experts, sparse activation ensures that only the most relevant experts (determined by the router) are utilized during the forward pass, thus optimizing computational efficiency.

Routing Mechanism: The routing mechanism in MoE layers, typically a softmax gating function, is responsible for allocating input tokens to different experts. It involves passing the input through a linear layer to produce logits, applying a softmax function to generate a probability distribution, and then using this distribution to select and weigh the contribution of each expert in processing the input.

Low-Rank Adaptation and its quantized successor QLoRA open this short series on the training and fine-tuning advances that reshaped large language models between 2023 and 2025.

The motivating intuition behind LoRA is that although a pretrained weight matrix W0 is large, the update needed to specialize a model for a new task tends to have low intrinsic rank, so most of the adaptation signal lives in a small subspace. [00275]
Rather than learning that update directly, LoRA factorizes it as the product of two much smaller matrices, B of shape d×r and A of shape r×k with r far smaller than min(d,k), and freezes W0 entirely. [00275]
The forward pass through an adapted layer becomes h = W0x + BAx, so training touches only A and B while the base model's weights never need gradients computed or stored. [00275]
B is initialized to zero and A to a random Gaussian, which guarantees the update BA is exactly zero at the start of training. [00275]
Because W0 + BA can be recombined into a single matrix before deployment, and swapped for a different B′A′ pair for another task, LoRA lets one base model serve many specialized adapters at minimal storage overhead. [00275]
QLoRA extends this by first compressing the frozen base model to 4-bit precision using NormalFloat4, a data type whose quantization bins are concentrated near the centre of the weight distribution to suit the roughly Gaussian shape of pretrained weights. [03514]
To limit the resulting error, QLoRA computes a separate quantization constant for every block of weights rather than one constant per tensor, and then quantizes those constants themselves in a second pass, called double quantization, trimming memory further without materially hurting accuracy. [03514]
It also relies on gradient checkpointing and paged optimizers to keep activation-gradient memory from spiking while gradients flow through the frozen quantized weights into the still full-precision adapters, which remain the only parameters actually updated. [03514]
The practical payoff of this pair of techniques is that models once requiring multi-GPU clusters to adapt can be fine-tuned on far more modest hardware, with task-switching costing megabytes of adapter weights rather than a full checkpoint. [00275] [03514]
The open questions sit mostly in the knobs rather than the mechanism: choosing rank r trades approximation fidelity against overfitting when data is scarce, and deciding how aggressively to quantize the base model remains an active area for later variants.

Direct Preference Optimization is the second technique in this series, and it let alignment teams skip the reinforcement-learning stage of RLHF entirely.
Standard RLHF fits a reward model to human preference comparisons using the Bradley-Terry model and a classification loss, then runs an RL stage that maximizes that reward while a KL term keeps the policy near a reference model, a three-phase pipeline that is complex and often unstable. [02738]
DPO's central move is that the KL-constrained reward-maximization problem solved in the RL stage has a closed-form solution: the KL divergence between a candidate policy πθ(y|x) and the distribution (1/Z(x))πref(y|x)exp((1/β)r(x,y)) is, by Gibbs' inequality, minimized at zero exactly when the two distributions coincide, so the optimal policy π* is that normalized, reward-tilted reference distribution. [00100]
Because that optimal-policy expression is intractable to use directly, since Z(x) requires summing over every possible string, it is instead rearranged to write the reward itself as r(x,y) = β log πr(y|x)/πref(y|x) + β log Z(x), turning a statement about rewards into an equivalent statement about a policy and a reference policy. [02738] [00100]
Substituting this reparameterized reward into the Bradley-Terry preference probability p*(y1≻y2|x) = σ(r*(x,y1) − r*(x,y2)) makes the intractable Z(x) cancel out of the difference, leaving human preference probability expressed purely through the optimal and reference policies, with no reward model in sight. [02738] [00100]
That yields a maximum-likelihood objective directly over the policy's own parameters, trained via ordinary supervised learning with a negative log-likelihood loss over an offline dataset of prompts paired with a preferred and dispreferred completion sampled from the reference policy. [02738] [00100]
The benefit is threefold: no reward model needs to be trained, no reinforcement learning loop is required, and the language model is optimized on human preferences using a well-understood supervised procedure instead of a notoriously fragile one. [00100]
Its documented weaknesses include a dependence on paired preference data that is not always easy to collect, sensitivity to label noise since it cannot account for the chance a preference was flipped, and an inability to sample fresh preference pairs from the current optimal policy because it never fits an explicit reward model. [00829]
These gaps motivated follow-on methods including KTO, which drops the need for paired data by maximizing a Kahneman-Tversky value function over individually labeled desirable and undesirable examples, RSO, which uses statistical rejection sampling to better approximate preference data from the target optimal policy, and IPO and conservative DPO, which add mechanisms that resist over-optimizing away from the reference model during long training runs. [00829]

Mixture-of-Experts architecture is the third advance covered here, and it decouples a model's total parameter count from the compute spent per token.
The intuition is conditional computation: instead of pushing every token through one dense feed-forward block, an MoE layer keeps n parallel expert feed-forward networks and a gating network that outputs a vector G(x) scoring each expert's relevance to the current token. [01053]
The layer's output is a weighted sum of the experts' outputs, each weighted by the corresponding entry of G(x), and a top-K gating rule restricts this sum to only the K highest-scoring experts by applying a softmax to the top-K logits of a linear layer rather than to all n, so K can be far smaller than n while the model still holds the full parameter space. [01053]
Mixtral 8x7B applies this by giving each transformer layer eight expert feed-forward blocks in place of one, routing every token to its top two experts, and as a result the model carries 47 billion total parameters but activates only about 13 billion of them to process any given token. [01053]
Because each expert can be assigned to a different accelerator through expert parallelism, sparse MoE layers fit naturally onto multi-GPU training and serving. [01053]
The open challenge that remains squarely on the training side is load balancing: ensuring an even distribution of tokens across experts is necessary to prevent bottlenecks and to make full use of the available compute, and it is flagged as a genuine engineering concern rather than a solved problem. [01053]
